title: Out of the depths
hookLine: a psalm that starts at the bottom and waits for morning (Psalm 130)
carry: more than watchmen for the morning

lines: FOUR IN THE MORNING ON THE NIGHT SHIFT.
A PSALM BUILT LIKE THAT NIGHT.
cards: Four in the morning at a shut-up warehouse. The night guard walks the loading dock and looks east, over the rooftops. Still black.
He finishes his round, pours coffee from a flask, looks east again. Still black. Somewhere a dog barks.
Nobody on that shift can make the sun come up any faster. All anyone can do is keep watch, look east, and wait. There's a psalm built exactly like that night.

teach.b: First, from the bottom. Psalm one hundred thirty opens: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." No warm-up, no praise first.
The singer is already down there, calling up.
Second, no scorecard. Then a surprise: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared."
If God kept a strict ledger, nobody would be left standing, and the psalm answers its own question: there is forgiveness.
It's a different picture from the one Job's friends drew, where every suffering had a line in the ledger.

Third, waiting for morning. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning."
It says it twice, like someone looking east a second time. Another old translation puts it: more than watchmen for the morning. The watchmen can't hurry the dawn.
They can only keep watch, sure it's coming.

teach.h: A WEEK OF SPEAKING FROM INSIDE IT.
teach.b: Fourth, the week. Job lost everything, and the reader knew it wasn't deserved. His friends sat seven days in silence, then talked, and were wrong.
Job argued and asked for a hearing.

teach.h: MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR THE MORNING.
teach.b: The whirlwind answered with stars and hawks. Psalm thirteen asked how long. And now a cry from the depths, and a long wait for the light.
Not one of them explains suffering away. Each one finds a way to speak from inside it.

how: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 130, alone and in worship, and some people in both traditions turn to it in times of distress or grief.

o: night guards who wait for a dawn they can't hurry
soldiers who stand guard at a king's palace gate
workers who watch the sky to forecast the weather

p: they that watch for the morning

s: Psalm 130 begins with thanks and praise
it begins out of the depths, crying to the LORD.
the psalm says that if God marked every wrong, no one could stand
"who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee."
the psalm says the singer has already been lifted out
it says I wait, my soul doth wait, more than they that watch for the morning.

games.q: you're the singer of Psalm 130, crying out of the depths. you've just asked: if God marked every wrong, who could stand? what comes next?
o: a list of your own wrongs
but there is forgiveness with thee
games.why: the psalm answers its own question: there is forgiveness with God, and then it waits for the LORD like watchmen for morning.

practice: Find the lowest place in you right now, deep or just a little low, and don't climb out of it yet; keep watch from there, the way the guard does.

On each in-breath look east, in your mind, toward where the light will come; on each out-breath let the dark be dark a little longer. If your attention wanders, look east again, the way the psalm says its line a second time.

wordCard.voice: Watchmen, from Psalm one hundred thirty's ending: waiting for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, watchmen who cannot hurry the dawn. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: out of the depths, the opening word of Psalm 130 after its heading.

carryVoice: Your line: more than watchmen for the morning. A week of voices speaking from inside suffering. Day seven hundred fourteen, and a week, done.
